questions.topic: What loose equality does to a string holding only white space
questions.learningObjective: predict the result of comparing a blank or padded string with a number using == rather than ===
questions.practice: tracing loose equality against numbers
questions.stem:
The script runs, in order, on one line separated by semicolons, and prints each result:
`console.log('' == 0, ' ' == 0, '0.0' == 0, '00' == 0, '0x10' == 16, '1e2' == 100, ' 12 ' == 12, '12abc' == 12, 'abc' == 0)`
The actual output is the nine booleans in that order. Which line of output did the program really print?

options.text: true true true true true true true false false
true true false false false false true false false
options.misconception: believes a padded or exponential string is not converted to a number by ==

options.text: false false false false true true true true false
options.misconception: believes == refuses to convert either side and only compares types

options.text: true true true true true true true true true
options.misconception: believes a non-numeric string still compares equal to zero because both are falsy

questions.explanation: When one side of == is a number and the other is a string, the string is run through the same conversion the Number function performs: trim the ends, then read the whole remainder as a numeric literal. So '' and ' ' both trim to nothing, which the engine reads as zero, and '0.0' and '00' are complete literals for zero, which is why all four are true. '0x10' is a complete hexadecimal literal and '1e2' is a complete exponential one, so they convert to 16 and 100. ' 12 ' trims to '12', which is complete, so it is 12. '12abc' and 'abc' are not complete literals, so both convert to NaN, and nothing is ever equal to NaN. The trap is that the conversion is a parse, not a scan, and the strict operator refuses to do it at all: `'' === 0`, `'0.0' === 0` and `' 12 ' === 12` are all false because a string is never strictly equal to a number.
questions.hint: Trim each string, then ask whether what is left is a complete numeric literal; only an incomplete one becomes NaN.

questions.topic: Why a boxed primitive is never strictly equal to its own value
questions.learningObjective: trace equality between a primitive and the object that wraps it
questions.practice: tracing primitive against boxed comparisons
questions.stem:
A script declares `const boxed = new Number(5);` and then runs:
`console.log(boxed == 5, boxed === 5, typeof boxed, Object(5) === 5, [5] == 5, [5] === 5, boxed.valueOf() === 5)`
The program prints those seven results in that order. What did it print?

options.text: true true number true true true true
options.misconception: believes the wrapper is transparent because the loose comparison already unwrapped it

options.text: false false object false false false false
options.misconception: believes an object never compares equal to a primitive under either operator

options.text: true false object true true true false
options.misconception: believes an array or a Number object is strictly equal to a primitive of the same value

options.text: true false object false true false true

questions.explanation: new Number(5) produces an object whose internal value is 5, and an object is never strictly equal to a primitive because the two are different kinds of thing, so boxed === 5 is false and typeof boxed reports object. The loose operator is willing to convert, and converting the object runs its valueOf, which hands back the primitive 5, so boxed == 5 is true. Object(5) is the same wrapper written as a conversion, so it is an object too and is also not strictly equal to 5. An array is an object as well, which is why [5] == 5 is true while [5] === 5 is false, and why [5] == '5' is also true. The last expression is the honest test: calling valueOf yourself hands you the primitive back, and a primitive is strictly equal to the same primitive.
questions.hint: Decide for each expression whether the two sides are the same kind of value before asking whether they match.

questions.topic: Why the plus operator concatenates as soon as one side is a string
questions.learningObjective: trace the arithmetic operators against a string operand and predict each result
questions.practice: tracing the plus, minus and times operators
questions.stem:
A script runs:
`console.log(1 + 2, '1' + 2, 1 + '2', '5' - 2, '5' * '2', '5' + null, true + 1, '1' - 1, '10' + 20 - 5)`
The values are printed in the order written. What does the program print?

options.misconception: believes a numeric string still takes part in addition as a number
believes a null operand is dropped from the concatenation

options.text: 3 12 12 NaN NaN 5null 2 0 1015
options.misconception: believes any string operand makes every operation in the expression textual

questions.explanation: Plus is the only one of the three that has two jobs. If neither operand is a string it adds, so 1 + 2 is 3. If either operand is a string it concatenates instead, turning the other operand into text first, so '1' + 2 and 1 + '2' are both the two-character string 12, and '5' + null is '5null' because null is written as its own name. Minus and times have no such branch: they always convert their operands to numbers, so '5' - 2 is 3 and '5' * '2' is 10. A boolean operand is not a string, so true + 1 adds and gives 2, while '1' - 1 still subtracts after conversion and gives 0. The last expression shows left-to-right evaluation doing the deciding: '10' + 20 concatenates to '1020', and only then does the minus strip it back to a number, so the answer is 1015 and not the 25 that a right-to-left reading would produce.
questions.hint: Check operand types one operator at a time; plus changes behaviour when a string is present and the other two never do.

questions.topic: How the two empty values behave under each equality operator
questions.learningObjective: compare how null and undefined respond to loose and strict equality and to ordering
questions.practice: tracing null and undefined comparisons
questions.stem:
A script runs:
`console.log(null == undefined, null === undefined, null == 0, null == false, null == '', null > 0, null <= 0, null < 1, null >= 0)`
Nine booleans are printed in the order written. Which line did the program actually print?

options.text: true false true true true false false false false
options.misconception: believes the empty values convert to zero for comparison and ordering

options.text: true false false false false false true true true
false false false false false true true false true
options.misconception: believes null is strictly equal to undefined because both mean absent

options.text: true true true false false true true true true
options.misconception: believes the two empty values are the same value under every operator

questions.explanation: Loose equality has one special case, and it is exactly this pair: null equals undefined and nothing else. So the first result is true and the second, the strict comparison, is false because they are two distinct values. The other three are false because the special case does not generalise: loose equality does not turn the empty values into zero, false or the empty string, so null == 0, null == false and null == '' are all false. Ordering has its own rule. When one operand is null and the other is a number, the number is converted to zero, but the comparison keeps the null on the left, so null > 0 is false while null <= 0, null < 1 and null >= 0 are all true. That is a one-sided conversion, and it is the reason a null is not smaller than everything: it is treated as zero and only zero, so it compares as equal to zero and as larger than nothing else below it.
questions.hint: Separate the one loose-equality special case from the separate rule that governs ordering against a number.

questions.topic: The two typeof results that surprise people most
questions.learningObjective: predict typeof for the values whose result does not match the writer's expectation
questions.practice: tracing typeof over the value kinds
questions.stem:
A script runs:
`console.log(typeof null, typeof undefined, typeof NaN, typeof [], typeof /re/, typeof (() => {}), typeof new Number(1), typeof notDeclaredAnywhere)`
Eight words are printed in that order. Note that the file is an ES module, so its code is strict. What did the program print?

options.text: object undefined number object object function object undefined
null undefined number array regexp function number undefined
options.misconception: believes typeof reports the name the value was written with rather than its internal kind

options.text: object undefined number object object function object referenceError
options.misconception: believes a name that was never declared throws when typeof is applied to it

options.text: object null number object object function object undefined
options.misconception: believes typeof undefined prints the text null because both mean absent

questions.explanation: typeof reports one of a fixed set of words, and two of them are counter-intuitive. null is a primitive, yet typeof null is object: the test that would separate objects from functions cannot tell an ordinary object from the value named null itself, and the specification froze the answer as object rather than change a result the web depends on. NaN is a number in every way that matters, so typeof NaN is number and only a comparison reveals it is not a usable one. Arrays and regular expressions are objects, so they report object and not array or regexp, and typeof a function is function. The last one is the useful exception: typeof on a name that was never declared returns undefined instead of throwing, which is exactly what makes typeof safe for feature detection. Reading that name in any other position, without typeof in front of it, throws a ReferenceError.
questions.hint: Typeof can only return the words in its fixed list; check which values fall into a bucket that surprises the writer.

questions.topic: Why a value that is not a number cannot be found by an equality search
questions.learningObjective: trace a search for a value that is never equal to itself and pick the search that finds it
questions.practice: searching an array for a not-a-number value
questions.stem:
A script holds `const xs = [1, NaN, 3];` and runs:
`console.log(NaN === NaN, xs.indexOf(NaN), xs.includes(NaN), xs.find(v => v === v), xs.filter(v => !Number.isNaN(v)), Math.min(...xs))`
Six results are printed in order. What did the program print?

options.text: true 1 true 1 1,3 NaN
options.misconception: believes an identical value compares equal to itself even when it is not a number

options.text: false 1 false 1 1,3 1
options.misconception: believes every array search uses the same comparison, so they all agree

options.text: false -1 true undefined 1,3 NaN
options.misconception: believes a test for value equality can never match the not-a-number value

options.text: false -1 true 1 1,3 NaN

questions.explanation: Not-a-number is the one value that is not equal to itself, which sounds like a joke and is instead a design decision: the arithmetic that produces it is where the failure happened, so refusing to let it pass a later equality check stops a bad value from being mistaken for a good one one. That is why indexOf, which compares with strict equality, reports -1 and never finds it. includes uses a different comparison, one that treats not-a-number as equal to itself precisely so that a list of numbers can be searched, so it returns true. A hand-written test written as v === v is the same mistake as indexOf and never matches, which is why the filter using Number.isNaN correctly returns just 1 and 3. The last one is a different trap: passing not-a-number into a minimum or maximum makes the whole result not a number, because a function that cannot reduce its inputs reports failure rather than skipping the bad one.
questions.hint: Ask whether each search compares with strict equality or with the comparison that treats not-a-number as matching itself.

questions.topic: Where consecutive integers stop being distinct
questions.learningObjective: compute the largest integer a number type can hold exactly and predict where sums stop changing
questions.practice: tracing integer limits
questions.stem:
A script runs:
`console.log(Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, 9007199254740993, 9007199254740992 + 1 === 9007199254740992, 9007199254740991 + 1, 123456789012345678 + 1)`
Five numbers are printed in that order. What did the program print?

options.misconception: believes an integer literal keeps every digit it was written with
believes the safe integer limit is the first integer that stops being exact rather than the last that is
believes adding one to two to the fifty-third power still produces a distinct value

questions.explanation: Every number a script works with is a double-precision binary value, and it stores a sign, an exponent and a fixed number of fraction bits, so the whole and fractional parts share one budget. That budget buys fifty-three bits of binary significand, which is nine quadrillion seven hundred fifteen trillion and change: two to the fifty-third is nine quadrillion seven hundred fifteen trillion nine hundred and ninety-two, and the largest integer that can be told apart from its neighbour is one less than that, which is what the constant reports. Past that point adjacent integers collapse onto the same value, which is why the literal written as two to the fifty-third plus one prints as two to the fifty-three, and why adding one to it does not change it and the comparison against the unchanged value is true. The final result is the same fact seen from the other side: an eighteen-digit number is already too large, so the trailing digits of the sum are rounded rather than carried.
questions.hint: Work out the value of two to the fifty-third and compare it with the printed constant before reading the rest.

questions.topic: Why one tenth added to one fifth is not one third
questions.learningObjective: compute the error in a decimal sum and choose a comparison that tolerates it
questions.practice: tracing a floating point sum and its tolerance
questions.stem:
A script runs:
`const s = 0.1 + 0.2; console.log(s, s === 0.3, s.toFixed(2), Math.abs(s - 0.3) < Number.EPSILON, 0.1 * 3, (0.1 * 3).toFixed(2), (0.1 + 0.2).toFixed(17))`
Seven results are printed in that order. What did the program print?

options.misconception: believes decimal fractions are stored exactly, so the sum returns the written value
believes the absolute difference exceeds the smallest representable gap between two numbers
believes toFixed reports every digit the value actually holds

questions.explanation: Numbers are stored as binary fractions, and one tenth has no exact binary form: the nearest representable value is slightly above one tenth, and one fifth is slightly above that. Adding them adds the errors as well, so the sum lands one gap above the nearest value to three tenths, which prints as 0.30000000000000004 and is not strictly equal to 0.3. The error is tiny, and the fourth result shows the standard way to accept it: compare the difference against the smallest gap between representable numbers near one, and this gap is well under that, so the test passes. The fifth result is the same defect arriving by multiplication, and the sixth shows the real point of toFixed, which is formatting for a human at a fixed number of places rather than revealing the stored value. The seventeenth-digit print is the honest one, and it is the number the equality test was actually comparing.
questions.hint: The difference between the sum and three tenths is far smaller than the smallest gap between neighbouring numbers near one; compare the two.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: What an integer parser keeps and what a number conversion refuses
questions.learningObjective: compare the two string-to-number functions on the same inputs and predict each result
questions.practice: tracing parseInt against Number
questions.stem:
A script runs:
`console.log(parseInt('12px'), Number('12px'), parseInt('px12'), parseInt('  42  '), parseInt(''), Number(''), parseInt('1e3'), Number('1e3'), parseInt('101', 2), Number('101', 2))`
Ten results are printed in order. What did the program print?

options.misconception: believes both functions read a leading number and stop at the first character that is not one
believes a trailing non-numeric suffix makes the whole conversion fail in both functions

options.text: 12 NaN NaN 42 NaN NaN 1 1000 5 NaN
options.misconception: believes an empty string is not a number in either function

questions.explanation: The two functions have different contracts, which is why mixing them is a bug factory. An integer parser reads digits from the front and stops at the first character it cannot use, so '12px' gives 12 and 'px12' gives nothing at all because there is no leading digit. A number conversion has no stopping rule: the whole trimmed string has to be a valid numeric literal, so '12px' is rejected and reported as not-a-number. Whitespace is trimmed by both, so '  42  ' is 42 either way, but the empty string separates them: the integer parser has nothing to read and fails, while the number conversion treats no text at all as zero. Exponential notation is the clearest difference, since a parser reads the leading one and stops at the letter, giving 1 where the conversion gives 1000. A radix argument is only meaningful for the parser, so Number('101', 2) ignores the two and reads the digits as decimal, giving 101, while the parser reads them in base two and gives 5.
questions.hint: Decide for each function whether it stops at the first unusable character or demands that the whole string be a number.

questions.topic: Which base an integer parser assumes and when it does not
questions.learningObjective: predict how an integer parser reads a prefixed or zero-padded literal
questions.practice: tracing radix handling in an integer parser
questions.stem:
A script runs:
`console.log(parseInt('0x1f'), parseInt('010'), parseInt('08'), parseInt('0b101'), parseInt('0o17'), +'0b101', +'0o17', Number('0x1f'), Number('1f'))`
Nine results are printed in that order. What did the program print?

options.misconception: believes a leading zero still selects octal in current practice
believes a leading zero means base zero and so always fails
believes a number conversion reads the digits after a prefix in the same base the prefix names

questions.explanation: An integer parser with no radix argument assumes base ten, with one exception: a leading zero followed by x is recognised as hexadecimal. So '0x1f' is read as thirty-one either way, because a base given explicitly as sixteen produces the same number. A leading zero on its own no longer means octal, so '010' is ten and '08' is eight rather than a parse failure, which is the change that removed a long-standing surprise. The binary and octal prefixes are not part of the parser's contract, so the parser reads the leading zero, stops at the letter and returns nothing: both '0b101' and '0o17' give zero. The unary plus is a different function altogether, and the number grammar it uses does understand both prefixes, so the same two strings give five and fifteen. That is the practical hazard: the same text read by two conversions gives two different numbers with no error raised by either.
questions.hint: One of these two functions stops at the first character it cannot read; work out which of the four prefixed strings it cannot finish.

questions.topic: Which strings a number conversion accepts as zero and which it rejects
questions.learningObjective: predict the result of converting blank, textual and structural values to numbers
questions.practice: tracing the number conversion across value shapes
questions.stem:
A script runs:
`console.log(Number(''), Number(' '), Number('x'), Number('1_2'), Number('true'), Number('0b11'), Number(null), Number(undefined), Number(true), Number([]), Number([7]), Number([1,2]), Number({}))`
Thirteen results are printed in order. What did the program print?

options.text: 0 NaN NaN NaN NaN 3 NaN NaN 1 NaN 7 NaN NaN
options.misconception: believes a string of only white space is not a valid number while an empty one is

options.text: NaN NaN NaN NaN NaN 3 0 NaN 1 0 7 7 NaN
options.misconception: believes an array converts by joining its elements into one number

options.text: 0 0 NaN NaN NaN 3 0 NaN 1 0 7 NaN NaN
0 0 NaN 12 NaN 3 0 NaN 1 0 7 NaN NaN
options.misconception: believes an underscore between digits is a digit-group separator the parser understands

questions.explanation: Converting a string trims it and then requires the whole remainder to be a valid numeric literal, and the empty remainder counts as zero. That is why both the empty string and a string of nothing but a space give zero, while any non-numeric text gives the failure value, and an underscore is not a digit separator in the string grammar even though it is a digit separator in numeric literals, so '1_2' fails. Words that name numbers do not help either, so 'true' is rejected while the boolean itself converts to one. The non-string values take a different route: the empty values are handled first, so the empty value converts to zero and the other one to failure, and a boolean converts by being one. Arrays and objects go through their own string form. The empty array stringifies to nothing and so becomes zero, a single-element array stringifies to that element and becomes seven, a two-element array stringifies to '1,2' which is not a number, and an object stringifies to bracketed text which is not a number either.
questions.hint: Strings go through the numeric literal grammar after trimming; everything else goes through its own string form first.

questions.topic: Why one empty value adds up and the other does not
questions.learningObjective: trace arithmetic and string building against the two empty values
questions.practice: tracing arithmetic with absent values
questions.stem:
A script runs:
`console.log(null + 1, undefined + 1, null - 1, undefined - 1, null * 5, undefined * 5, '' + null, '' + undefined, String(null), String(undefined))`
Ten results are printed in order. What did the program printed?

options.text: 1 1 -1 -1 0 0 null undefined null undefined
options.misconception: believes the two empty values are treated the same way in arithmetic

options.text: 1 NaN -1 NaN 0 NaN null undefined null undefined
0 0 0 0 0 0 null undefined null undefined
options.misconception: believes the empty value placeholder converts to zero for arithmetic

options.text: 1 NaN 1 NaN 0 NaN undefined undefined null undefined
options.misconception: believes concatenating onto an empty string concatenates the empty values as their own names

questions.explanation: Arithmetic has a rule for one empty value and no rule for the other. The value named null converts to zero before any arithmetic operator touches it, which is why adding one gives one, subtracting one gives minus one and multiplying by five gives zero: the arithmetic is silently treating an absent reading as a real zero reading. The other empty value has no numeric meaning at all, so every arithmetic result becomes the failure value instead, and a total built from it is useless without being told. String building is a different route again and converts the other way, through the value's own text: the value named null writes as its own name and the absent one writes as its own name, so an empty string in front of either produces a four-word or a nine-letter result rather than a number. Turning the values into text deliberately produces exactly the same two words, which is the quick way to confirm the mechanism.
questions.hint: Decide which operator branch each expression takes before deciding which value is converted.

questions.topic: What a bitwise operator does to a value wider than thirty-two bits
questions.learningObjective: trace the truncation a bitwise operator performs and the wrap-around it produces
questions.practice: tracing bitwise truncation and shifts
questions.stem:
A script runs:
`console.log(2147483648 | 0, 4294967296 | 0, -1 >>> 0, -1 >> 1, -1 >>> 1, 5 & 3, 5 | 3, 5 ^ 3, 5 >>> 1, 1 << 31)`
Ten numbers are printed in that order. What did the program print?

options.misconception: believes a bitwise operator keeps the value unchanged and simply drops the fractional part
believes the unsigned shift leaves a negative number negative
believes a left shift of one past the sign bit produces a large positive number

questions.explanation: Every bitwise operator first converts its operands to thirty-two-bit integers, and any higher bits are discarded, which is why the largest power of two that fits in a signed thirty-two-bit integer comes back as the negative value at the other end of the range. Discarding high bits is not the same as discarding value: a power of two beyond the range is made of nothing but the bits that were discarded, so it arrives as zero. The shift family has two separate operators and the difference between them is the sign. The right shift that keeps the sign fills from the left with copies of the sign bit, so minus one stays minus one however far it shifts. The unsigned right shift treats the bits as unsigned, so minus one becomes the largest unsigned thirty-two-bit value, and one to the left of zero becomes a value with every bit but the lowest set. The last result is the sign bit being set: one shifted left into bit position thirty-one produces a negative number, not a large positive one.
questions.hint: Reduce each operand to thirty-two bits first, then decide which kind of shift fills from the left.

questions.topic: Which rounding function a negative decimal needs
questions.learningObjective: compare the rounding and truncation functions on a value with a fractional part
questions.practice: tracing rounding functions on negatives
questions.stem:
A script holds `const v = -3.7;` and runs:
`console.log(Math.trunc(v), Math.floor(v), Math.ceil(v), Math.round(v), ~ ~v, parseInt(v), Number(v.toFixed(0)), v | 0, [-3.7, 3.7].map(Math.trunc), [-3.7, 3.7].map(Math.floor))`
Ten results are printed in that order, ignoring the space in the double tilde. What did the program print?

options.misconception: believes truncation and the floor function always agree
believes rounding to the nearest integer always rounds a negative fraction towards zero
believes the nearest-integer function rounds a half away from zero in both directions

questions.explanation: The two families answer different questions. Truncation removes the fractional part and keeps the sign, so minus three point seven becomes minus three, and the two-element list confirms it: mapping truncation over a negative and a positive gives minus three and three. The floor function instead rounds towards minus infinity, so it gives minus four for the negative and three for the positive, and mapping it over the same list gives minus four and three. The ceiling rounds the other way, and for this value it lands on minus three, the same as truncation by coincidence rather than by rule. Nearest-integer rounding splits at the half and sends a negative half downwards, so minus three point seven rounds to minus four, which is why the list shows minus four here and the final expression shows that a half written as two point five rounds away from zero while a negative two point five rounds to minus two. The formatting and parsing routes are the ones that surprise: toFixed formats for display and rounds the formatted text, giving minus four, while the integer parser discards the remainder and gives minus three.
questions.hint: Sort the functions into two groups, those that keep the sign and those that round towards minus infinity, and check each against a positive and a negative.

questions.topic: Where a property read comes from when the object does not have it
questions.learningObjective: trace a property read down the prototype chain and identify which link answered
questions.practice: tracing property lookup across a prototype chain
questions.stem:
A script builds an object whose prototype holds two properties:
`const proto = { role: 'reader', team: 'core' }; const o = Object.create(proto); o.role = 'owner';`
It then runs:
`console.log(o.role, o.team, 'role' in o, Object.hasOwn(o, 'role'), Object.hasOwn(o, 'team'), o.hasOwnProperty('team'), Object.keys(o))`
Seven results are printed in order. What did the program print?

options.text: owner core true true true true [ 'role', 'team' ]
options.misconception: believes a property the object can read is therefore a property the object owns

options.text: reader core false true false false [ 'team' ]
options.misconception: believes a property written on the prototype is hidden once the object sets its own

options.text: owner core true true false false [ 'role' ]
owner core true true false false [ 'role', 'team' ]
options.misconception: believes the key list includes every property a read can reach

questions.explanation: A read walks the chain: the object first, then its prototype, then whatever that prototype inherits. The first read finds the value the script wrote on the object, so it reports the owner's role; the second finds nothing on the object and continues up, so it reports the inherited team. The two questions after that ask different things and that is the whole distinction. The in operator asks whether the chain has the key at all, so it is true. The own-property test asks only whether the first link has it, so it is true for the role the script wrote and false for the team it inherited, even though reading team worked perfectly. The method call agrees, because that method asks the same question, and the key list is the direct enumeration of the object's own enumerable keys, which contains only the one name the script wrote. The last expression in the program shows the practical consequence: deleting the own role leaves the object readable at that name again, because the inherited value takes over.
questions.hint: Separate the three questions: does the chain have the key, does this object own it, and what does a read return.

options.misconception: believes keys are compared field by field

options.text: Both object lookups find their own entry, the third finds nothing, the primitive lookup finds nothing, and the size is two
options.misconception: believes the bad-value primitive cannot be used as a key

options.text: The first lookup finds its entry, the second overwrites it, the third finds that entry, and the size is two
options.misconception: believes two structurally equal objects collide as keys

options.text: Both object lookups find their own entry, the third finds nothing, the primitive lookup finds its entry, and the size is three

What does each function return?

options.text: The first returns the try value, the second and third return the finally value, and the fourth returns the value assigned in the finally

Later, a handler is attached to the same promise and it does receive the error. What is happening, and where is the smallest place to fix it?

options.text: The promise was already resolved, so the later handler received a stale value rather than the error
options.misconception: believes a promise that rejected can still be resolved

questions.topic: Why the loose equality operator is the wrong one for a value read off a control
questions.learningObjective: explain the class of bugs produced by coercing an unvalidated text value in a comparison

questions.stem: A form has a field the developer expects to hold a number and a checkbox the developer expects to hold a yes-or-no. The validation is written with the loose equality operator in both places, and the page has shipped. Explain why both checks behave the way they do, what class of input each one lets through, and what the fix costs.

answer.exemplar: Loose equality does not compare the two values the developer thinks it is comparing. It first converts one side, and which side it converts depends on the types it finds, so the result is a statement about the converted values rather than about what the user typed. For the number field the conversion turns the text into a number before comparing, and the text conversion trims the ends and then requires what is left to be a complete numeric literal. That makes the rule surprisingly permissive: an empty field trims to nothing, which reads as zero, so an empty submission satisfies a check against zero, and so does a field containing nothing but spaces. A value of twelve with a unit suffix is rejected, which is correct, but a value with a trailing zero written as zero point zero is accepted, and a value written in hexadecimal or exponential form is accepted, so the set of accepted inputs is the whole numeric-literal grammar rather than the decimal digits the developer had in mind. For the checkbox the conversion runs the other way: the control arrives as text, so comparing it to a boolean means converting the boolean, and the text is then read for truthiness. An empty string, a zero, a whitespace-only string and the bad-value number are all falsy, so all of them satisfy a check against false, and a field the user never touched is indistinguishable from a deliberate no. The two checks are wrong for the same reason and in opposite directions, which is what makes the pair instructive: one is too permissive about what counts as a number and the other is too permissive about what counts as no. The cost of the fix is small and worth naming. A text field has to be converted once, deliberately, at the point the data enters the program, and the conversion has to be a total function that either produces a number or a stated failure, rather than a conversion that quietly produces the failure value and lets the comparison decide what that means. Once that is done, the rest of the program can compare numbers with numbers and booleans with booleans, and the validation message can name the field that is wrong instead of reporting that a value is not what it was expected to be. The alternative of keeping the loose comparison and adding more cases to it is the design that produces the bug report, because every new accepted format is a new branch nobody remembers to extend.

Reaching for the general advice to use strict equality without working through the empty string, the whitespace-only string and the hexadecimal form leaves the item unanswered, because those are exactly the cases that decide whether the check is right.

questions.topic: Why a copied object can still be changed from outside the copy
questions.learningObjective: explain the lifetime a one-level copy gives to the values it shares with its source
questions.practice: explaining shared state after a one-level copy
questions.stem: A reducer keeps its state in a value it updates by copying the outer object and replacing one property. A test that copies the same way reports that a nested value changed even though the copy was supposed to be a new snapshot. Explain what the copy does and does not detach, how a change made through one path becomes visible through the other, and what it would take to be safe.

answer.exemplar: A copy written with the spread operator detaches exactly one level and no more. It walks the source's own enumerable properties and writes each value into a fresh object; where a value is itself an object, what gets written is the reference, not a copy of it. So the new object is genuinely new as an object, which is what the reducer relies on when it compares the previous state with the next one and sees a different reference, and the values inside it are the same values as before, which is what makes a change made through the source visible inside the copy. There is only ever one nested object in that picture, so there is nothing for the copy to be independent of. Two failure shapes follow from this, and they pull in opposite directions. The first is silent aliasing: code holding the copy mutates a nested value and expects the source to be untouched, and the source has changed too, so two parts of the program end up editing the same data. In a reducer that produces a wrong result rather than a crash, because the previous state was already modified by the time anything compared it, so a change that should have produced a new state produces a mutated old one. The second is the missed change: the reducer replaced only an outer property, the nested value was edited in place, and the comparison of old against new reports no change because the outer references are equal where they were equal and the nested one was never compared. A general deep copy would fix the first shape and create the second, because a deep copy makes every nested value a new reference and the equality check then reports a change on every render, which is why frameworks warn against deep comparison in this position. The arrangements that actually work are all about ownership rather than about copying. Keeping the nested values immutable makes a change mean a replacement, so the only way to change one is to write a new one, and the copy is safe because the values it holds will never be edited. Normalising the nested data into its own keyed collection, with each nested row addressed by a stable key, gives every value exactly one owner and turns the aliasing question into a question about who is allowed to write that key. Comparing on something other than reference works when the data is small enough that a structural comparison is cheap, but it has to be written as an explicit decision, because the default comparison is identity and identity is exactly what the copy preserved.

questions.explanation: A model answer has to establish that the copy is new at one level and shared below that, trace a single nested change through both paths, and then confront the trap that a deep copy fixes the aliasing and breaks the change detection at the same time. Offering only the advice to copy more deeply misses the second half, because the reason the code compares references is the same reason the one-level copy is safe to compare.
questions.hint: Ask which properties of the copy are new objects and which are the same objects as before, then ask what the state comparison is for.

questions.topic: What a serialisation round trip destroys and what it silently changes
questions.learningObjective: explain the losses produced by writing an object to text and reading it back
questions.practice: explaining the cost of a serialisation round trip
questions.stem: A service serialises a value to text and a client reads it back. The client finds that a date is now text, a lookup table is now an empty object, a function is gone, a key that held the unready value is gone, and two numbers that should have stayed distinct both arrived as the same value. Explain each of the five changes, and say which of them the client can detect and which it cannot.

answer.exemplar: A text format is a tree of names and values, so anything that is not a name or a value in that sense has to be translated, and anything that cannot be translated has to be dropped. That single constraint explains all five changes. A date is an object, and its day and month are not own enumerable properties of it: they are internal slots reached by method calls. The serialiser has a specific instruction to look for a method that produces a string and to use it, so the date is written as text, and the reader has no way to know the text was a date unless the format says so. A lookup table is a different case of the same problem. Its entries live inside the object as a separate list rather than as properties, so there is no own property to write, and the result is an object with the right shape and none of the contents, which is the most dangerous of the five because nothing about it is malformed. Functions and the unready value are dropped outright: the format describes data, and neither is data. A function has behaviour, and behaviour cannot be reconstructed from a name; the unready value has no representation in the tree at all. Both therefore disappear, and the reader cannot distinguish a key that was dropped from a key that never existed, which matters whenever the reader uses the presence of a key to decide whether a field was supplied. The two numbers that collapse are the quietest failure. The format writes each number using the shortest decimal text that reads back as the same stored value, and the reader parses that text back to a number by the same rule, so a round trip is faithful to the stored value and not to the value that was written. Where the reader's parser rounds differently, or where the text is processed in between, two distinct values arrive as one. The detection question is the useful part of the answer. The dropped keys and the collapsed numbers are detectable, but only against a record of what was sent, which the receiver does not have. The date, the empty lookup table and the missing functions arrive looking like well-formed data of a different shape, so a receiver has no signal at all unless the contract told it what shape to expect and it checks. That is the argument for putting the type information in the contract, at the boundary, rather than hoping the shape survives on its own.

questions.explanation: A model answer has to give a reason for each of the five changes rather than listing them, and has to separate the losses the receiver can detect from the ones it cannot. Concluding that serialisation loses information is not enough, because the item is about which losses are visible and why some of them are not.
questions.hint: Ask what the text format is able to express, and for each of the five values ask whether it is a name, a value, or neither.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Why a module that imports a name can observe a value the exporter has already changed
questions.learningObjective: explain what an imported name refers to and how that differs from a copy
questions.practice: explaining a live view between two modules
questions.stem: Two modules import each other. The first keeps a counter and a function that raises it. The second reads the counter and reports what it saw. A driver calls the raising function, then asks both sides what they see, and both report the new value. Then the second module is changed to read the counter at its top level instead of inside a function, and importing either module throws before the driver runs. Explain the first behaviour and the second, and say what each says about the design.

answer.exemplar: The first behaviour follows from what an import actually is. The imported name is not a copy of the exporting module's value; it is a reference to the exporting module's binding, and every read goes back to the exporter for whatever the binding holds at that moment. That is why the second module reports the new count after the first module's function raised it, and why there is no synchronisation problem to think about: there is one value, owned by one module, and the second module is a second reader rather than a second writer. A snapshot would behave differently, and the difference is what makes this worth understanding rather than memorising. With a snapshot, the second module would carry its own variable initialised once at import time, so it would report the old count forever unless something explicitly refreshed it, and a counter read through a snapshot would be a different counter from the one the exporter is maintaining. The second behaviour is the price of the rule, and it is about evaluation order rather than about reading. A module body runs when it is imported, and when two modules import each other the engine has to pick one to evaluate first; whichever it picks second will run its body while the first is still part-way through, and if the second body reads a name the first body has not yet assigned, that read happens in the window where the binding is entered but not ready. Reading it there is an error, not a value, and the error surfaces as soon as the import is evaluated, which is why it appears before any of the program's own code runs. Both observations point at the same design rule. Keep module bodies free of reads of imported mutable values, and put the reads inside functions so they happen after evaluation has finished. Where a genuine cycle is unavoidable, the shape that works is for the modules to expose functions and hold no state that the other reads during evaluation, so the only shared thing is a call. The cost of ignoring the rule is a failure that appears at import time with a message about a name rather than about the logic, which is one of the harder failures to diagnose because nothing in the program's own code has run yet.

questions.explanation: A model answer has to explain the first behaviour in terms of what an imported name refers to, and the second in terms of the order module bodies are evaluated when two of them form a cycle. Saying that a cycle is not allowed is wrong and will be marked as such, because the item is precisely about what a cycle is allowed to do.
questions.hint: Ask what the importing module is holding, and then ask which module body the engine evaluates first when two of them import each other.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Ordering the steps that produce the receiver and the arguments of a call
questions.learningObjective: sequence the observable steps that happen between reading a callee and entering its body
questions.practice: ordering the steps of a call
questions.stem: A program logs each observable step of `obj.target(argA, argB)`, where reading the property logs a line, each argument's conversion logs a line, and the body logs a line naming its receiver. The log, in the order the program produced it, is: read the property, convert the first argument, convert the second argument, enter the body. Put these five steps in the order a call actually performs them, naming which step is the one that would change if the callee were fetched through a longer property chain.

options.text: Evaluate the object expression the property is read from, which is the step that lengthens when the chain is longer
Bind the arguments to the parameters and enter the body, where the receiver is the object the property was read from
Evaluate the property access on the left of the call and read the callee, so the property is fetched before anything else happens
Evaluate the arguments left to right, converting each as it goes, and record the receiver to be passed in
Call the resulting function value with the recorded receiver and the converted arguments

questions.explanation: The order exists to explain one thing: why the object on the left is the receiver even when the property is fetched through a chain, and why an argument that throws does so before the body ever runs. The object expression is evaluated first, which is the step that grows with a longer chain, so in a chain of two the first object is evaluated and its property read before the second object is even looked at. Reading the callee comes next, and only then are the arguments evaluated, left to right, each one converted at the point it is evaluated, so a conversion that throws stops the call before the body is entered. The arguments and the receiver are then bound to the parameters and the body runs. Putting the argument step before the property read is the misconception that makes side effects appear in the wrong order, and putting the body before the arguments is the one that hides a conversion failure inside a method.
questions.hint: Ask which evaluation the argument list depends on, and remember that an argument is evaluated where it is written.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Ordering the conversion steps of a loose comparison between text and a number
questions.learningObjective: sequence the conversions a loose comparison performs before it decides
questions.practice: ordering the steps of a loose comparison
questions.stem: A program compares the text '  12px  ' with the number zero using the loose operator, and each of the five things that happen is logged. The log, in order, is: read both operands with no conversion yet; decide which side to convert because one is text and the other is a number; trim the leading and trailing white space off the text; parse the trimmed text as a decimal literal and find that it is not one, producing the failure value; and decide that the failure value is not equal to zero. Put these five steps in the order the engine actually performs them, naming the step that would be skipped for a strict comparison.

options.text: Trim the leading and trailing white space off the text, leaving twelve point p x as the candidate
Parse the trimmed text as a decimal literal, and because what is left is not a complete literal the result is the failure value
Compare the two results, and since the failure value is not equal to zero the comparison is false
Read both operands, with no conversion applied to either one yet
Because the two operands are of different kinds and one is text, choose which one to convert, which is the step a strict comparison skips entirely

questions.explanation: The order matters because two of these steps are the whole difference between the two operators, and because the trimming step is where a surprising class of inputs is decided. Nothing happens at the first step: both operands are read exactly as they are, and no conversion is attempted, which is the state the strict operator stops in forever. The second step is the branch the loose operator takes and the strict one does not, and it is a decision about kinds rather than about values, so it happens even when both sides would convert to the same number. Trimming is the third step and it is the one that makes blank input comparable at all, because an empty or whitespace-only field trims to nothing, and nothing is read as zero. Parsing is the fourth, and it is a parse rather than a scan, so a partial match is not accepted and the result is the failure value. Only then is the comparison made, and the failure value never equals anything, which is why the whole sequence exists in order to produce a false answer from an input that looks almost like a number.
questions.hint: Ask what the strict operator does, and use that to find the step it never reaches.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Ordering the path a rejected promise takes before anyone handles it
questions.learningObjective: sequence what happens to a failure in an async function up to the point a handler can see it
questions.practice: ordering the path of a failure to a handler
questions.stem: A program calls an async function that throws, attaches nothing to the returned promise, and ends its synchronous work. The host reports an unhandled rejection at the end of the turn. A handler is then attached from a timer in a later turn and it does receive the error. Put these five observations in the order they occur, naming the one that explains why a late handler still works.

options.text: The throw settles the promise the call returned with a rejection, and the call itself succeeds, so the caller receives a perfectly good promise
The synchronous work of the caller finishes, and at the end of that turn the host reports the rejection as unhandled
A handler is attached later and still receives the same rejection, because the rejection was recorded on the promise rather than consumed by the report
The report is cleared and nothing further is observed, so the failure is gone even though the value was never lost
The call enters the async function and its body runs up to the throw

questions.explanation: The order is what makes the failure invisible in the first place, and it is the reason a handler attached later still works. The throw inside the async function does not escape to the caller as a synchronous exception, because the function has already committed to returning a promise, so the first two steps are that the body runs and that the throw becomes a rejection on the promise the call returns. The call itself therefore succeeds, and a caller that treats the call as the operation has a false picture: the operation is still in flight and has already failed. The caller's synchronous work then finishes with nothing attached, and the host notices at the end of that turn, which is the earliest point at which the engine can know that no handler was attached during the turn. The last two steps are the ones that matter for the fix. The rejection was recorded on the promise, and the report was only an observation, so a handler attached in a later turn still receives the same rejection, which the run confirms. Nothing was lost and nothing was consumed; the value was simply unattended, and attaching a handler anywhere on that path still works. That is why the fix is a handler rather than a change to the reporting.
questions.hint: Ask whether the throw escapes the function, and ask whether the report consumes the rejection or only observes it.
